title: KaleidoKV: Rearranging Evidence for Efficient KV Cache Reuse in Offline RAG Inference
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) augments large language models (LLMs) on question-answering (QA) tasks with retrieved evidence at inference time. Related questions in an offline batch often retrieve overlapping evidence, but prefix caching reuses key-value (KV) states only for identical token prefixes, making reuse dependent on evidence order. Although all questions and evidence are known before execution, existing reordering methods commit to early grouping decisions and can miss sharing opportunities that require several requests to move together. Evaluating alternative layouts can incur planning costs that offset inference savings, while concurrent requests may still recompute shared prefixes before their KV states become available. To address these challenges, we propose KaleidoKV, a framework that plans evidence orders across the batch and controls when requests enter the engine while preserving each request's evidence set and content. Joint layout planning revises formed groups through coordinated request moves and keeps a move only if it lowers planned prefill, the computation required when each shared prefix is computed once. A global prefix index selects evidence orders by locating reusable prefixes and evaluates each move incrementally from only the affected request paths. Prefix-ready admission tracks nested prefix dependencies, delaying requests whose shared prefixes are still being computed while allowing independent requests to proceed. Experiments on four QA workloads and four LLMs show that KaleidoKV achieves the highest throughput and lowest mean time to first token in all 16 settings, with approximately 1.24-1.75x the throughput of the strongest baseline, including planning time. With Llama-3.1-8B under the default configuration, actual prefill stays within 0.5% of planned prefill across all four workloads.

title: Read Boundaries in Agent Memory: Consistency, Completeness, and Repair
comment: Accepted by IEEE CCWC 2027
summary: Agent-memory services assemble evidence through several reads across connections or stores. An update between those reads can pair an assertion with source content from another revision. We protect the complete recall, including enrichment and materialization, and evaluate the resulting evidence and service behavior in Hindsight and Cognee. A 600-run Cognee study compares unprotected recall, a repeated recall, a read/write lock, and optimistic epoch validation under default incremental updates and full rebuilds. At approximately 20 recalls/s, unprotected default updates yield 199 conflicting responses among 12,010 scheduled recalls with spaced writes and 284 among 12,010 with bursts. The lock and epoch validation each deliver complete, compatible evidence for all 24,020 default-update recalls. With default bursts, epoch validation reduces update p95 by 109 ms while adding 290 ms to recall p95 relative to the lock. A separate 160-run incremental-failure study distinguishes mixed revisions from complete new derived content whose canonical source record remains old. Both protected policies refuse service after failure; the first default retry restores all 80 fault runs through native full-rebuild fallback. In Hindsight, a shared PostgreSQL snapshot removes the mismatch in ten controlled pairs, with recall p95 rising from 19 ms to 29 ms. These results identify the read boundary needed for coherent evidence and the publication and recovery conditions governing service after an update fails.

title: CapCover Filter: Semantic Approximate Membership Queries over Embeddings
summary:
Determining whether an embedding is sufficiently similar to any vector in a vector store without performing a nearest-neighbor search can substantially improve query throughput in vector-store systems. We study Semantic Approximate Membership Queries (SAMQs), which allow queries to be rejected when no indexed vector meets the requested similarity threshold, while guaranteeing no false negatives.
  We introduce CapCover Filter, a geometric data structure that summarizes a set of embeddings using spherical caps. Its representation is independent of the query threshold, allowing a single filter to support arbitrary thresholds without reconstruction. We evaluate alternative construction and quantization methods, compare CapCover Filter with competing filters, and measure its impact on query throughput.
  Across five real-world datasets, at a cosine similarity threshold of 0.95, CapCover Filter eliminates approximately 20--100\% of index accesses while using only 2\% of the raw (FP32) embedding memory. When placed before a FAISS flat index, it improves query throughput by up to 382\% and by approximately 116\% on average across the five datasets, while returning the same range-search result. We also evaluate lower similarity thresholds. Our results show that CapCover Filter can substantially improve vector-store throughput when similarity thresholds are tight, retrieval is expensive, and indexed embeddings are highly clustered. We release an optimized implementation of CapCover Filter and its evaluation framework.

title: Optimizing Query Decomposition for Reliable Validation
comment: 20 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) have made querying databases more accessible, but cannot guarantee that the SQL they generate is correct. Without a trusted reference query, a validator (human or LLM) must decide whether a generated query answers the intended question. Enterprise questions often require queries with multiple joins, nested subqueries, and multi-level aggregation, and validating such a query in one judgment is error-prone. Decomposition simplifies this task by rewriting a query into smaller queries (blocks) that recompose to the original, each checked against its own sub-question.
  Decompositions differ, however: smaller blocks make each judgment easier but require more judgments, and the best balance depends on the validator's ability. We formulate validation-aware query decomposition as an optimization problem. Just as a query optimizer chooses among equivalent plans by estimated cost, we choose among decompositions by how reliably a given validator is expected to check them. We model how task difficulty and validator ability jointly affect reliability and define an objective that balances reliability against the number of judgments. Over a space of decompositions derived from logical-plan rewrites, our search finds an optimal one. We implement it in DecoVal, a pipeline that presents each block with its sub-question and input interface, combines local verdicts into a query-level decision, and localizes errors to blocks.
  A user study shows that decomposition helps human validators catch and locate errors: with DecoVal, participants caught 91% of the errors, up from 36% without decomposition, and located the error in nearly every rejection. Experiments on BEAVER and Spider 2.0 with LLM validators show that DecoVal also raises error-detection recall over whole-query validation while keeping precision high, and that the best granularity depends on the validator.

title: A Gaussian Primitive Data Management Framework for Efficient 3DGS Trajectory Rendering
summary: Trajectory rendering, which renders novel views of a reconstructed 3D scene along a camera path, is a core operation in digital twins and autonomous inspection. Structured 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) renders a single view in real time by decoding sparse anchors into Gaussians on demand, but it renders a trajectory view by view: every view projects all anchors to select them, re-decodes anchors already requested by neighboring views, and runs all steps on the GPU while the CPU idles. We treat this as a spatial data management problem, where anchors are spatial objects, views are range queries, and decoded Gaussians are shared derived data, and propose GDM-GS, which removes redundancy at three levels. Within a view, an anchor index and an occluder index answer each view as a holed-frustum range query, so out-of-view and provably hidden anchors are never decoded. Across views, shared materialization decodes each requested anchor once per group of consecutive views while preserving each view's selection. Across processors, a hybrid pipeline balances selections between the CPU and the GPU before grouped decoding under bounded memory. Experiments on large-scale public scenes show that GDM-GS substantially reduces trajectory rendering latency while preserving image quality.

title: QuarkDB: A Hybrid Database System for Quantum Data Management
comment: 14 pages, 12 figures, Submitted to ICDE2027
summary: Emerging quantum applications like quantum communication generate large volumes of high-dimensional quantum data, requiring efficient data analysis and storage. However, classical database systems often struggle to meet requirements such as quantum processing or version management. This paper presents QuarkDB designed for efficient quantum data management. QuarkDB establishes a unified object model for relational and quantum data and defines the syntax of Quantum Structured Query Language. To support efficient quantum data management, QuarkDB integrates three key components: (1) a Hybrid Query Engine with cost-based hybrid plan selection over classical and quantum operators, (2) an Execution Engine with a three-level instructions intermediate representation, QuarkDB-IR, to support quantum execution and reduce quantum processing costs, and (3) a Storage Engine supporting quantum data version management, state reconstruction and data reuse. Compared with classical databases such as SQLite and PostgreSQL or quantum databases like Qute, our QuarkDB achieves query-latency speedups ranging from 2.14x to 25.86x speedup under extensive real-world workloads.

title: Tight Width Minimisation of Self-Join-Free Quantified Conjunctive Queries
comment: To appear at PODS 2027
summary: Query minimisation is a classical problem in database theory and the width of a formula, defined as the maximum number of free variables over all subformulae, is a central measure for query evaluation. We study width minimisation for a subclass of quantified conjunctive queries (QCQs), namely self-join-free QCQs. For this subclass, we show that rewriting optimality coincides with semantic optimality: given a query $φ$, the minimum-width query obtainable from $φ$ by applying natural and established rewriting rules has minimum width among all first-order formulae logically equivalent to $φ$. As a consequence, the width of a self-join-free QCQ can be optimised by a logical-equivalence-preserving rewriting algorithm.

title: Adaptive-Elbow Graph Traversal for Schema Retrieval in Text-to-SQL
comment: Presented at the 5th Italian Conference on Big Data and Data Science (ITADATA 2026). To appear in CEUR Workshop Proceedings
summary: LLM-based natural-language interfaces to relational databases are gated by a schema-retrieval step: the generator can only be as good as the slice of schema it is shown. On a database with hundreds of tables, that slice must be selected and the selection is two-sided---omit a needed table and the query becomes unrecoverable, include too many and the irrelevant ones act as noise that degrades the model's output. When an agentic retriever that lets the model inspect the schema can be too costly or too slow, the fallback is an embedder that ranks tables by cosine similarity and keeps a top-k. This fallback has two weaknesses: a fixed budget is suboptimal question by question, and embedding similarity overlooks foreign-key-linked tables that are necessary for joins. We present Adaptive-Elbow Graph Traversal (AEGT, ElbowHop for short), a property-graph table retriever that addresses both: an adaptive elbow cutoff replaces the fixed budget with a per-question one under a single aggressiveness parameter, and bidirectional foreign-key traversal deterministically recovers the bridge tables embedding similarity misses. We evaluate the retriever on 3 corpora of increasing candidate-pool size (BIRD Mini-Dev queried per database, 3--13 tables; its eleven schemas merged, 74; and a merged Spider-train graph, 546) and isolate the two mechanisms under a per-question budget-matched protocol. Across these settings the adaptive elbow emerges as the dominant mechanism---at matched recall it roughly doubles precision over a fixed budget on the larger pools, the margin widening as the pool grows---while the foreign-key traversal pays off on the join-critical bridge tables dense retrieval cannot reach, in the single-hop tight-budget case. We characterize the method as a low-cost, recall-robust first stage for schema retrieval on which a downstream selection or generation step can build.

title: eFaaS: A Lightweight, Kernel-Bypass Serverless Framework for HPC Workloads
summary: The expanding scale and complexity of HPC workflows demand elastic resource provisioning and fine-grained concurrency, which serverless computing theoretically suits. However, existing serverless frameworks, optimized for lightweight event-driven applications, are architecturally mismatched for highly concurrent HPC. For HPC workflows, high concurrency necessitates spawning a large number of function instances, which entails substantial instance startup overhead and data transfer requirements. The kernel-based isolation and inter-instance communication mechanisms (via network stacks, cgroups, etc.) cause extra overhead—excessive kernel locks from cgroup/namespace configuration, and prolonged latency from cross-node data copying/serialization. To address these limitations, this paper proposes a novel serverless system architecture tailored specifically for HPC workflows. Leveraging eBPF, we design user-space lock-free isolation and end-to-end zero-copy communication mechanisms, thereby bypassing kernel involvement as much as possible. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that eFaaS stabilizes performance under extreme concurrency, reducing long-tail delays and achieving end-to-end speedups ranging from 1.27× to 3.74× on representative HPC workflows.

title: DolphinRouting: Cluster-Level Binary Routing for Disaggregated LLM Inference Serving
summary: Prefill-decode (PD) disaggregation isolates the two phases of large language model serving, but request-level path selection must account for prefill work, cache reuse, and decode demand. We present DolphinRouting, which learns this choice from end-to-end SLO feedback under a given P/D resource allocation. Requests are clustered by raw prompt length, cache-adjusted input lengths on both worker pools, and output-length information. Offline policy search learns one binary action per cluster. Online feature extraction, cluster assignment, and table lookup select local or remote prefill. We evaluate DolphinRouting on a real PD-disaggregated cluster using three public benchmarks, a mixed workload, and real data. Across the mixed workload and real data, DolphinRouting with -means reduces P90 TTFT by 5.7--7.9\% and P90 TPOT by 2.6--10.1\% relative to Dynamo.

title: Accelerating GPU Datalog with Kernel Fusion
summary: Recursive Datalog queries such as transitive closure, connected components, and same generation iterate a rule to a fixpoint while expressing many graph analytics. GPU Datalog engines run each round as a chain of separate relational operators driven by a host loop, paying for repeated sorting, per-round allocation, and a CPU↔ GPU round-trip every round. We present MONOLOG, which runs each round as a single CUDA kernel over one GPU-resident data structure, so a single CUDA atomic operation per derived fact deduplicates, tests novelty and adds the fact together. With the state staying on the device, the whole loop runs on the GPU via a replayed CUDA graph and a conditional graph node. As these queries only grow under edge insertions, a computed result is updated in place when edges arrive. On an NVIDIA A100 this cuts end-to-end time by up to 24× for transitive closure and 136× for connected components over the MNMGDATALOG engine, beats GPULOG by up to 29× in fixpoint compute, and updates connected components up to 40× faster than recomputing.

title: Dynamic Planning for Scalable Data Movement in Accelerated Query Engines
summary: At scale, structured-data processing is often a datamovement problem. Joins and aggregations must choose whether to shuffle, broadcast, or reduce intermediate results, and the right choice can depend on data properties that are hard to predict prior to execution. In this paper, we introduce dynamic planning, a query-optimization method that lets operators choose data-movement strategies at runtime. We have implemented this approach in GPU Polars, where RapidsMPF actors observe table chunks and exchange metadata before selecting a strategy. Controlled microbenchmarks and a PDS-H Q9 case study confirm that dynamic planning makes sensible runtime decisions while preserving both stability and performance.

title: Amortized Cell-Probe Lower Bounds for Dynamic Boolean Problems
summary: We prove the first unconditional amortized cell-probe lower bound for a Boolean dynamic problem. For insert-only multiphase Disjointness with query sets over and word size , a fixed distribution of interleaved insertions and queries forces this expected average cost per operation, excluding preprocessing. The bound allows sufficiently small constant error for each query of every fixed legal sequence and imposes no restriction on individual operation costs. It transfers to incremental directed reachability, incremental subgraph connectivity, and fully dynamic triangle detection. We also prove for amortized insertion time and expected query time , when the number of insertions before the final query is not announced in advance. We reach the quadratic-logarithmic scale with bounded error by combining interleaving with the 2.5-round communication framework [Ko26a, Ko26b] and controlling errors among accepted simulations.

title: An Engineering Approach to Explainable Artificial Intelligence for SQL Query Optimization: Design and Evaluation of the OptiMind Framework
summary: OptiMind was evaluated using benchmark and enterprise workloads, including JOB, IMDB, SQLShare, Spider, and enterprise traces. Experimental results demonstrate that the framework reduces mean absolute error (MAE) by 18.4%–31.7% compared with PostgreSQL’s native optimizer and achieves execution speedups ranging from 1.31× to 2.14× on complex multi-join queries. Additionally, OptiMind achieved an interpretability score of 4.51/5.0, confirming strong explanation quality, recommendation usefulness, and practical effectiveness for transparent, workload-adaptive, and explainable SQL query optimization in modern database systems.

title: Data Optimization Study of Genetic Algorithm and Machine Learning
summary: The genetic algorithm (GA) is a widely used evolutionary computing method in computer science, management, physics, engineering, and other domains. The study demonstrates that evolutionary algorithms may effectively answer a wide range of research issues, including query optimization, work scheduling, data mining, part-of-speech tagger, phrase chunker, image segmentation, inventory management, etc. In machine learning (ML), the two processes of improving datasets to improve model performance and using algorithmic optimization to enable models to learn effectively from that data are referred to as data optimization. It covers everything from the actual data storage and cleanup to the mathematical adjustments made to model parameters during training. Both GA and ML perform better than the traditional techniques when it comes to data optimization. GAs are search techniques that optimize complex machine learning problems by imitating natural selection. When gradient-based methods fail, they use selection, crossover, and mutation to iteratively evolve possible solutions in order to find optimal parameters or designs. This study aims to maximize the data and demonstrate the use of genetic algorithms with machine learning in several computer science fields.

title: Schema-Conditioned Tree-Mamba For Database-Agnostic Cost Estimation Under Schema Shift
summary: Accurate cost estimation is central to query optimization, but learned estimators must generalize when a trained model is deployed on databases with unseen schemas and data distributions. Existing database-agnostic methods typically expose catalog statistics or table-level evidence as static input features, leaving child-subplan fusion rules fixed and agnostic to schema uncertainty. We develop a probabilistic schema-conditioned Tree-Mamba estimator in which soft schema-pattern posteriors control child-state fusion. A train-only SchemaVAE and Bayesian information criterion (BIC)-selected Gaussian mixture model derive table-level schema posteriors from PostgreSQL catalog and workload statistics; these posteriors are propagated through each physical plan tree and used by a relation gate that composes left and right subtree states. On a 20-database benchmark with four unseen-database folds, the proposed fusion mechanism achieves the best aggregate Median, P95, and P99 Q-error among representative baselines, and ablations confirm that conditioned fusion is more effective than hard clustering or posterior concatenation.

title: Adaptive data processing using a machine learning mechanism
summary: The relevance of this topic stems from the rapid growth in the number of heterogeneous and unstable data sources in modern information systems. Under such conditions, traditional approaches to organizing information retrieval no longer ensure sufficient efficiency, as they do not account for changes in the availability of sources, their response times, and the quality of the results obtained. The problem becomes particularly relevant in event-driven architectures, for which there are currently no universal mechanisms for adaptive control of the search process and selection of data sources. The increasing volume of publications requires innovative solutions that directly impact the quality of the results obtained and the overall efficiency of computational resource utilization. The aim of this article is to develop and implement reinforcement learning algorithms in event-driven systems to solve problems of adaptive evaluation and selection of data sources. To achieve this goal, an adaptive selection mechanism based on the Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) [9], [13] algorithm has been developed. An approach is proposed for forming a source state vector and a reward function based on behavioral and content metrics. This allows the system to dynamically adapt its search strategy depending on the characteristics of the query and the effectiveness of the sources in real time. Unlike static meta-search strategies, the developed system is capable of independently adapting to environmental changes during operation. A simulation environment was created, the results of which confirmed the unquestionable advantage of the adaptive approach: balance is achieved between result quality (increased relevance) and costs (reduced processing time and elimination of duplicates).Keywords: adaptive source selection, event-driven systems, machine learning, reinforcement learning, Soft Actor-Critic, asynchronous data processing, ranking, deduplication, distributed search systems, reward function, state vector, action vector, scientific information aggregation, semantic search, relevance, dynamic control, query optimization, metasearch systems.

title: Probe-Based Routing for Join Optimizer Selection
summary: In optimizers that choose a join-order solver by a size rule, join ordering is an algorithm-selection problem, because dynamic programming (DP), genetic search (GEQO), and Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) each win on different queries. PostgreSQL nevertheless chooses among them by relation count alone, although queries with the same relation count can favor different solvers. This paper introduces two landscape features that a probe computes from random join orders in microseconds per query. The tail spacing describes how the costs of the best sampled orders are spaced, and the crossover surprise describes how far the cost of a crossover child deviates from the mean cost of its parents. The router clusters training queries by these features and the relation count, assigns a solver to every cluster that this solver wins in total end-to-end time by a margin, and leaves all other queries to PostgreSQL's default rule. On JOB and IMDb-CEB, the router lowers mean end-to-end time relative to the default rule, and on IMDb-CEB the probe features nearly double the gain obtained from the relation count alone, so they carry information about the queries that the relation count lacks.

title: Secure Explainable AI Framework for Privacy-Aware Digital Healthcare Marketing Data Analytics
summary: Artificial Intelligence in Digital Healthcare Marketing offers great promise for personalized patient engagement, however, data privacy, model interpretability, and regulatory compliance are important challenges. In this paper, we propose an optimized secure and explainable AI framework for healthcare marketing, combining federated learning with differential privacy mechanisms to guarantee data localization and robust privacy assurances. It contains a query fragment caching algorithm to enhance the analytical performance while maintaining privacy protection, and it adds SHAP and LIME techniques to ensure model transparency. Experimental results on a large healthcare marketing dataset show that the proposed approach obtains 92.4% accuracy and a privacy budget of with an interpretability score of 0.87. The comparative analysis shows that the framework provides a 37.2% faster query response time and a 28.6% lower risk of privacy leakage than the existing frameworks, confirming the feasibility of implementing a privacy-aware, explainable artificial intelligence system in healthcare marketing settings with regulatory requirements.

title: Machine learning in fiber-reinforced composites: A review of modeling, lifecycle applications, and challenges
summary: Fiber-reinforced composites (FRCs) are critical in aerospace, automotive, and deep-sea infrastructure. However, their multi-scale heterogeneity poses significant challenges to traditional methods. Machine learning (ML) offers a transformative approach for FRC lifecycle management. This review systematically examines recent ML advancements in the FRC domain, covering data acquisition, model architectures, lifecycle applications, and challenges toward industrial deployment. Statistical analysis reveals textual data constitutes approximately 3.2 times the volume of image data, primarily from experimental testing, numerical simulation, and stochastic modeling, underscoring the necessity of multi-source data fusion. Three advanced models are critically reviewed: physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), optimization algorithm-fused neural networks (OAFNNs), and ensemble learning models (ELMs). Their applications are analyzed across lifecycle dimensions: structural design and performance prediction, manufacturing and machining process optimization, and damage detection with structural health monitoring. Key challenges include data scarcity, generalization under distribution shifts, the simulation-to-reality gap, and limited cross-material and cross-environment validation, alongside issues of computational cost, model interpretability, and uncertainty quantification. Finally, future directions are outlined, encompassing next-generation physics-data hybrid methods, multi-source heterogeneous integration, integrated digital twin and self-sensing systems, and enabling technologies for industrial deployment. This review provides a comprehensive technical reference for transitioning ML from laboratory validation toward reliable engineering deployment.

title: A Cost-Effective Zero-Knowledge Proof-Enabled Framework for Verifiable Collaborative Learning in Resource-Constrained Digital Twin Networks
summary: Digital twin networks (DTNs) continue to rely on collaborative learning to facilitate improved performance across distributed users. Ensuring model updates integrity and trust in such settings, however, remains a critical challenge, particularly in the presence of malicious participants. While zero-knowledge proofs (ZKPs) offer strong guarantees for verifiable computation, the associated high computational and energy overhead make such approaches impractical for resource-constrained clients. This paper thus proposes a cost-effective zero-knowledge verification framework for DTNs. The design adopts a lightweight client-side commitment with server-side ZKP-enabled security to support learning within DTNs. To further reduce overhead, a probabilistic proving mechanism is introduced with an adaptive control strategy to dynamically optimize verification frequency. A comprehensive cost model, as well as overall system efficiency, is then developed for the system. Results demonstrate that the proposed framework significantly reduces cost compared to conventional ZKP approaches while meeting the required threat detection accuracy and high system efficiency. The framework offers a practical pathway toward secure and scalable federated intelligence in next-generation DTNs.

title: How Reliable Is Learned Cardinality Estimation? A Data Model-Centric Analysis and Empirical Study
summary: Learning-based cardinality estimation (CE) has emerged as a promising alternative to statistics-based techniques. Yet its reliability remains an open question: directional bias, upper-tail risk, and degradation under data or workload shifts. Existing works typically organize learned CE by learning paradigm, such as query-driven versus data-driven, which can obscure how the underlying data model constrains estimator design and reliability. We adopt a data model-centric perspective, introducing a unified analytical framework spanning query encoding, data feature extraction, and model adaptation. We argue that the most informative classification axis shifts across data models: primary modeling target for relational CE, topology-handling strategy for graph CE, and cross-model integration strategy for multi-model CE. A relational case study grounds this analysis: a topmost-join probe of PostgreSQL reveals systematic underestimation; a five-seed evaluation with checkpoint reuse across workloads characterizes MSCN’s workload-shift degradation; and a matched JOB-light comparison shows that learned estimation can substantially reduce, but does not eliminate, typical and tail errors. We further assess what current benchmarks reveal about reliability and identify open challenges toward robust, transparent, and reliable cardinality estimation.

title: Strategic Causal Policy Learning with Manipulable Eligibility
summary: The standard rule in unconstrained causal policy learning is simple: treat individuals with nonnegative CATEs. But this rule can fail when treatment eligibility is strategically manipulable. After a policy is announced, individuals may change the covariates used for assignment without changing their underlying treatment effects. We study how such responses affect treatment allocation and welfare. Using an access-burden representation, we characterize strategic treatment and decompose welfare loss into missed beneficial treatment and harmful treatment. For linear CATEs and quadratic manipulation costs, we derive closed-form threshold corrections. When manipulation costs are homogeneous, a single correction recovers the ideal positive-CATE allocation. With heterogeneous costs, welfare maximization, pointwise safety, and minimax group welfare regret can favor different thresholds. Simulations illustrate these tradeoffs and examine the effects of estimating treatment effects and behavioral responses.

title: Task offloading and joint resource optimization in Space-Air-Ground integrated vehicular networks
summary: Optimizing the allocation of computational and storage resources across ground, air, and space nodes in Space-Air-Ground integrated vehicular networks can effectively reduce vehicular task processing latency. To meet the low-cost offloading requirements of delay-sensitive tasks in Space-Air-Ground integrated vehicular networks, a task offloading scheme based on the Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient Algorithm with Recurrent Neural Network (TDR3) is proposed. First, the network transmission model, delay model, offloading cost model, and optimization problem model are constructed. Then, by comprehensively considering task processing delay and server cost, a TDR3-based deep reinforcement learning scheme is designed for task offloading and resource allocation. Finally, the proposed scheme is compared with Omni-DDPG, TD3, DDPG, RDPG, RNN-DRL, and the local computing scheme through comparative experiments. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed scheme achieves the same offloading success rate as Omni-DDPG and outperforms TD3, DDPG, RDPG, RNN-DRL, and the local computing scheme by 6.67%, 6.67%, 3.23%, 3.23%, and 357.15%, respectively, when the number of servers is 8 and the number of tasks is 35.

title: AI-Driven Portfolio Optimization Under Market Volatility and Transaction Constraints
summary: This research examines the problem of optimal portfolio construction in the presence of time-varying volatility, unstable correlations, and transaction costs - all features that lead to performance degradation of traditional mean-variance and risk-based optimization. Unlike previous researches, where volatility forecasting, portfolio allocation, and cost management were considered separately, this work proposes to consider all three elements as a unified process that includes LSTM-based volatility prediction, PPO-based reinforcement-learning portfolio allocation and threshold-based rebalancing taking into account transaction costs. The framework is tested on the dataset of 50 large-cap US stocks with the chronological train/validate/test split (2018-2022 / 2023 / 2024-2025), with Equal Weight, Mean-Variance, Risk Parity, Hierarchical Risk Parity and LSTM-only portfolio allocation serving as a baseline in similar conditions of transaction cost and rebalancing assumptions. In the out-of-sample test period (2024-2025), the proposed framework has achieved the following results: 14.2% annualized return, 15.9% annualized volatility, 0.87 Sharpe ratio and 20.7% max drawdown, with 1.00 and 0.77 being annual turn-over without and with cost-aware rebalancing correspondingly. Ablation and transaction-cost sensitivity analysis reveals the impact of the separate parts of the process. However, there are some important limitations of the presented results, such as current constituents' choice (risk of survivorship bias) and proportional transaction-cost model used.

title: Energy-efficient flexible job shop scheduling under time-of-use electricity pricing using a reinforcement learning-assisted evolutionary algorithm
summary: To address the difficulty of jointly optimizing production efficiency and electricity cost in flexible job shop scheduling under time-of-use electricity pricing, a bi-objective scheduling model is established to minimize the makespan and total electricity cost. An energy-aware hybrid reinforcement optimization algorithm (EAHROA) is proposed. The algorithm adopts a two-segment OS-MS encoding scheme to represent operation sequencing and machine selection. During decoding, a time-of-use electricity price-aware mechanism is introduced to calculate processing and idle electricity costs, guiding operations to avoid peak-price periods when possible. Three neighborhood structures, namely critical-machine reassignment, tariff-aware neighborhood search, and critical-operation insertion/swap, are designed to enhance local optimization for critical operations and high-cost operations. title: Neural Cipher Bench: Cost and Portability of Corner-ReLU Cipher Implementation
summary: Edge and Internet of Things (IoT) devices run neural networks on GPUs, neural processing units (NPUs), and microcontrollers (MCUs) through machine learning (ML) runtimes. Deep Neural Cryptography (DNC, EUROCRYPT 2026) expressed AES as a bit-exact ReLU network with fixed weights, using a corner-ReLU construction that keeps the cipher inside the affine+ ReLU operators such runtimes execute. What this construction costs on edge and IoT hardware, and whether real ML backends execute it correctly, had not been measured. We implement SM4, ARIA, Camellia, and ChaCha20 (spanning substitution–permutation, Feistel, and add–rotate–XOR structures) alongside AES on a shared corner-ReLU core under one construction policy, derive a cost model for width, depth, and neuron count, and measure five execution paths on four platforms. All ciphers admit bit-exact networks whose width and depth diverge with cipher structure, and the model's width predicted where GPU throughput drops. Every configuration passing the correctness check fell below its classical baseline (best 0.80×, SM4 on the GPU), by hundreds to thousands of times for the S-box ciphers on the MCU, and keeping the activations on chip through fusion raised throughput 1.4–3.5× and moved the peak past the predicted cache limit without closing the gap. Some AES configurations on the Apple Neural Engine returned valid-looking but incorrect outputs with no error or warning, a failure reproduced in a minimal graph without project code. Mathematical bit-exactness therefore does not guarantee backend-level bit-exactness, and exact workloads offloaded to edge NPUs require output validation.

title: SOVEREIGN-MOHAWK: Machine-Checked Hierarchical Byzantine Resilience and Probabilistic Composition for Federated Learning
summary: Federated learning (FL) at scale requires aggregating model updates across multi-tier topologies while tolerating adversarial participants. A pervasive foundational assumption in hierarchical FL design is compositional safety: if every local aggregation tier enforces an honest-majority guard (eg, Multi-Krum), the overall network inherits global Byzantine fault tolerance. In this paper, we present SOVEREIGN-MOHAWK, an FL architecture and LEAN 4 formal development that refutes and repairs this assumption. First, we present a machine-checked negative result: a concrete counterexample in LEAN 4 showing that naive deterministic composition of per-tier Multi-Krum guards fails, allowing a 60% global Byzantine leaf fraction to pass local filters under concentrated placement. Second, we formalize a probabilistic repair proving that under explicit iid Bernoulli committee sampling, the probability of any tier exceeding its Byzantine filtering threshold is strictly bounded by a Chernoff bound over rationals, verified in LEAN 4 using native_decide for T= 200 committees and c= 50, 000 leaves per committee (Pfail≤ 200× 10− 1000≈ 2× 10− 998). Third, we formalize eight core theoretical developments, including Rényi Differential Privacy (RDP) with constructivist rational logarithmic bounds, logarithmic pathdepth routing, MiMC permutation polynomials over BN254 scalar fields, Robbins-Siegmund supermartingale convergence, and post-quantum cryptographic (PQC) dual-signature migration non-hijack guarantees. Fourth, we couple these formal artifacts with an industrial Go production runtime and evaluate the system across multi-node Kubernetes-in-Docker (Kind) clusters (up to 500 pods), CI swarm matrices (500–1,500 nodes), and a 1,000-node simulator target under safe (10% Byzantine) and edge (35% Byzantine) adversarial regimes, demonstrating microsecond aggregation overhead (30.63 µs), sub-400ms round latency (373 ms at 1,500 nodes), and minimal accuracy impact (1.8% gap vs. clean baseline). Every formal claim is bound to implementation code via a continuous integration traceability pipeline.

title: Separations Between Submodular-Like Graph Widths
summary: Many algorithmic frameworks exist for evaluating join queries. Each of these frameworks except high-degree-low-degree splitting comes with a width notion of the query that determines its running-time exponent. We fill this gap by formalizing high-degree-low-degree splitting with degree classes, which gives rise to the degree-splitting width -width. These width notions form a hierarchy, but it was not known whether the more complicated frameworks achieve better worst-case exponents than the simpler ones on any graph query. We study this question for full self-join-free join queries with binary relations, which amounts to colored subgraph isomorphism for a pattern graph . title: MultiCard: Multiple Attribute Cardinality Estimation via Deep Learning
summary: Cardinality estimation is essential for query optimization, but most existing learned estimators focus on a single predicate type, such as string LIKE clauses or numerical range filters. In practice, analytical workloads often combine both types, while the accuracy of string estimators tends to decrease with longer patterns. We introduce MultiCard, a comprehensive learned cardinality estimator that unifies LIKE predicates and numerical filters within a single end-to-end architecture. By combining a Transformer for long-range sparse patterns with an LSTM for short, frequent patterns, MultiCard achieves robust pattern modeling. In parallel, a numerical encoder integrates catalog histograms and structural predicate features, enabling the model to dynamically assess histogram estimation accuracy across different operators and data skew conditions. A final Transformer layer captures interactions among heterogeneous predicates before a multilayer perceptron predicts query cardinalities. We also introduce UPCI, a workload generator that produces length-balanced LIKE patterns, multi-column numerical predicates, and exact cardinality labels for training and evaluation. Experiments on five real-world datasets show that, for string-only workloads, MultiCard achieves the best or near-best Q-error across all datasets compared with state-of-the-art methods. For mixed multi-attribute queries, MultiCard reduces PostgreSQL's mean Q-error by up to 16 times while maintaining an inference latency below 5 ms.

title: Towards Taming Data Comparisons in a Description Logic Setting
summary: We study a fragment of the query language XPath featuring data (in)equality operators, and its connection to Description Logics (DLs) with concrete domains. XPath has already been investigated from a Modal Logic (ML) perspective. Given the connection between ML and DL, it is only natural to examine XPath also from the DL viewpoint. To naturally capture data comparisons, we resort to DLs with concrete domains. In doing so, we establish an interesting connection between the two universes, from which we obtain transference results (e.g., complexity bounds for reasoning tasks). Furthermore, we refine complexity results and show that concept satisfiability, ABox consistency, and concept satisfiability w.r.t. a TBox are all NP-complete problems for the fragment of XPath under consideration. In this way, we obtain a DL fragment with data comparisons that features good computational properties.

title: Data Cleaning for Data Trees and Variants of Probabilistic Query Answering in an Epistemic Framework
summary: Graph-structured data is a common model for representing complex relationships that naturally appear in many domains, like social network analysis or data provenance. However, real-world data is often incomplete, contains errors, or is inconsistent with respect to certain properties we would expect it to satisfy. These restrictions can be written as integrity constraints in logical navigational languages, such as Regular Path Constraints or Reg-GXPath expressions. In this work, we continue the study of modeling uncertainty through a particular epistemic approach, where the observed data graph may contain mistakes or inconsistencies, which is a usual case when managing databases. This data graph will be considered a noisy version of a clean one that correctly models the world and is only known partially through a probability distribution over the universe of data graphs. We show that the Data Cleaning problem remains intractable even if we restrict it to data trees, evidencing that the epistemic model is too powerful and requires reasonable, tractable restrictions. We also study some variations of the Probabilistic Query Answering problem along with their corresponding complexity.

title: StepLens: Supporting Inspection and Evaluation in Agentic Tabular Data Work to Narrow Down the Gulf of Evaluation
summary:
Agentic systems can democratize data discovery and preparation by allowing users to express data needs in natural language and delegate workflows that would otherwise require substantial coordination across people, tools, and datasets. However, especially in high-stakes settings, answers are useful only when users can assess how they were produced.
We present StepLens, an interface layer built on Pneuma-Seeker, an agentic system for question answering over tabular data. StepLens organizes the system’s intermediate work into structured, inspectable stages, combining high-level summaries, artifact-level details, and lightweight interactions that help users trace and test how an answer was produced.
Through a formative study with 15 participants, we derive design insights into how users inspect and assess intermediate outputs. We then report a controlled experiment with 36 participants examining how the interface shapes confidence in the current answer, readiness to act on it, and overall trust in the system. Readiness to act was clearly differentiated between correct and incorrect answers under StepLens. Qualitative findings show structured visibility supported traceability and targeted inspection, but made inconsistencies more salient and sometimes complicated verification efforts.
